hws.subtitle: Ch. 6 — Empirical & Molecular Formulas, Percent Composition

hws.title: HW 15
hws.subtitle: Ch. 7 — Reaction Types, Balancing & Predicting Products

steps.html: Empirical formula = the smallest whole-number ratio of atoms ("easiest on the eyes").
Molecular formula = a multiple of the empirical one (it can still be divided down).
Test: look for one number (2, 3, 5…) that divides every subscript. If one exists → molecular. If none → empirical.
Pro tip: any subscript of 1 (written or understood) means it's always empirical.

atoms-in-moles.title: Atoms of one element in a sample

steps.html: Moles of that element = moles of compound × its subscript.
Compare the results; the largest is the answer.
Reduce the formula to its empirical form first.
Add the atomic masses from the periodic table, times each subscript.

mol-from-emp.title: Molecular formula from empirical formula + molar mass

steps.html: Find the empirical mass by adding atomic masses from the periodic table.
Factor = molecular mass ÷ empirical mass (should come out to a whole number).
Multiply every subscript by the factor.
Optional check: add up the new formula; it should match the given molecular mass.
% element = (mass of ALL of that element ÷ molar mass of the compound) × 100. Part over whole.
Top: atomic mass (periodic table) × its subscript.
Bottom: the whole molar mass, every element × its subscript, added up.
Divide, × 100, and round the way the problem says.

emp-from-data.title: Empirical formula from percents or grams

steps.html: Percents? Assume 100 g, so each percent becomes grams (82.66 % → 82.66 g).
If an element's amount isn't given, get it by subtraction (from 100 % or from the sample mass).
Turn each mass into moles: grams ÷ atomic mass from the periodic table. Do it for every element. Never use diatomic masses here.
Divide every mole value by the smallest one. This is the most-missed step.
Within 0.1 of a whole number → round. Ends in .5 → ×2; ends in .33 or .67 → ×3; ends in .25 or .75 → ×4. Multiply every element, not just the odd one.
Write the formula with the less electronegative element first (C before H before O; H never goes first except in acids).
Solute = the smaller amount, what gets dissolved. Solvent = the larger amount, what does the dissolving (usually water). Solution = the two mixed evenly (homogeneous).
Mass is conserved: solution mass = solute + solvent.
Dilute = more solvent (or less solute): lighter color, lower molarity. Concentrate = boil off solvent: solute stays the same.
Unsaturated = more can still dissolve. Saturated = at the limit (solid sits on the bottom). Supersaturated = heated then cooled, holding more than it should.
Molarity = moles of solute ÷ liters of solution (M = n/V).
It is written M, "molar", mol/L, or with square brackets [ ]. Molality is a different unit.
Rewrite any M as mol/L so you can see the two units cancel.
Volume must be in liters: mL ÷ 1000.
Grams ↔ moles uses the molar mass (given in the problem or from the periodic table).
Factor-label: start with the one-unit number (g, mol, L or mL), then chain the two-unit numbers (M, g/mol) so units cancel.
Sig figs: answer has as many as the least precise number (for × and ÷). Leading zeros don't count.
M₁V₁ = M₂V₂ (also written CV = CV). Concentrated on one side, dilute on the other.
Numbers joined by "of" (e.g. "20.0 mL of 1.69 M") go on the same side.
Both volumes in the same unit (both mL or both L).
Divide to isolate the unknown, then round to the right sig figs.
Seven elements always come in pairs: H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂ ("HOFBrINCl", the 7 shape on the table plus H).
Every other element is written as a single symbol (Na, K, Mg, C, Ne…).
Polyatomic ions come from the polyatomic ion chart (chlorite ClO₂⁻, sulfite SO₃²⁻, nitrate NO₃⁻…).
"-ide" means a single element ion (sulfide = S²⁻, chloride = Cl⁻).
Charges by column: +1, +2, Al +3 … −3, −2, −1; Roman numerals give a metal's charge.
Criss-cross charges so each compound is neutral, then balance with coefficients.
Combustion: fuel + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O. Look for it first.
Synthesis: only one product (no + on the right).
Decomposition: only one reactant (no + on the left).
Single replacement: an element by itself on each side, one swaps into a compound.
Double replacement: two compounds swap partners. If it makes a solid (s) it's also a precipitation reaction.
Atoms and mass are the same before and after a reaction. The number of molecules can change.
Balance with coefficients only. Changing a subscript makes a different substance.
1 mol = 6.022 × 10²³ particles. A subscript multiplies the atoms: 1 mol Cl₂ has 2 mol Cl.
Make a quick count of each atom on both sides.
Keep a polyatomic ion that appears on both sides as one group (count NO₃ as a unit).
Order: everything except H and O first, then H, then O last. Leave lone elements for the end.
A 2 and a 3? Swap them as coefficients. Odd number of O in combustion? Double the fuel and redo.
A coefficient multiplies everything in that formula. Recount at the end. eLearn wants a 1 typed in empty blanks.
Combustion → always CO₂ + H₂O.
Double replacement: keep the positives in place and swap the negatives.
Single replacement: the lone element takes the place of the matching ion (metal replaces metal).
Rebuild each new formula from its charges (columns + polyatomic chart). Never carry old subscripts over.
Then balance with coefficients (only if asked).

problems.q: Which one of the following is definitely not an empirical formula?

steps.html: Empirical = can't be reduced; look for a common factor in each set of subscripts.
C₄H₁₂N₂O: O = 1 → empirical. C₃H₈O₂: 3, 8, 2 share nothing → empirical.
C₁₂H₁₆O₃: 12, 16, 3 share nothing → empirical. C₁₂H₂₂O₁₁: 11 is prime and doesn't divide 12 → empirical.
C₆H₁₂O₄: 6, 12, 4 all divide by 2 → C₃H₆O₂, so it is molecular.

problems.q: Which contains the greatest number of carbon atoms?

steps.html: Moles of C = moles × carbons in the formula.
CO₂: 1.20 × 1 = 1.20 mol C. Al₂(CO₃)₃: 0.450 × 3 = 1.35 mol C (the 3 outside the parentheses).
Largest: 0.400 mol of C₄H₈O₂S.

problems.q: Select the empirical formulas below.

steps.html: C₅H₁₀: both divide by 5 → CH₂, so molecular.
C₃H₁₀: 3 and 10 share nothing → empirical.
C₃H₁₂: both divide by 3 → CH₄, so molecular.
C₂H₉: 2 and 9 share nothing → empirical. Answer: C₃H₁₀ and C₂H₉.

problems.q: Select the empirical formulas below.

steps.html: C₅H₁₀F₁₅: 5, 10, 15 all divide by 5 → CH₂F₃, so molecular.
C₂H₁₀Cl₅: 5 is odd, so 2 can't divide it → empirical.
C₃H₁₂Br and C₂H₉N₁₈: each has an understood or real subscript that blocks a common factor (Br is 1; 9 and 2 share nothing) → empirical.
Answer: C₂H₁₀Cl₅, C₃H₁₂Br, C₂H₉N₁₈.

problems.q: True or false: The empirical mass of C₂H₆ would be 15.04 g/mol.

steps.html: Reduce C₂H₆: both divide by 2 → empirical formula CH₃.
Molar masses (periodic table): C = 12.01, H = 1.01.

problems.q: The molecular mass of a compound with an empirical formula of SO₂ is 256 g/mol. What is the molecular formula?

steps.html: Molar masses (periodic table): S = 32.06, O = 16.00. Empirical mass SO₂ = 32.06 + 2(16.00) = 64.06 g/mol (≈ 64).
Factor = molecular ÷ empirical = 256 ÷ 64 = 4.
Multiply every subscript by 4: S₁ × 4, O₂ × 4 → S₄O₈ (typed S4O8).

problems.q: The molecular mass of a compound with an empirical formula of SO₂ is 192 g/mol. What is the molecular formula?

steps.html: Molar masses (periodic table): S = 32.06, O = 16.00. Empirical mass SO₂ = 32.06 + 2(16.00) = 64.06 g/mol (≈ 64).
Factor = molecular ÷ empirical = 192 ÷ 64 = 3.
Multiply every subscript by 3: S₁ × 3, O₂ × 3 → S₃O₆ (typed S3O6).

problems.q: The molecular mass of a compound with an empirical formula of SO₂ is 128 g/mol. What is the molecular formula?

steps.html: Molar masses (periodic table): S = 32.06, O = 16.00. Empirical mass SO₂ = 32.06 + 2(16.00) = 64.06 g/mol (≈ 64).
Factor = molecular ÷ empirical = 128 ÷ 64 = 2.
Multiply every subscript by 2: S₁ × 2, O₂ × 2 → S₂O₄ (typed S2O4).

problems.q: What is the percent by mass of hydrogen in C₂H₈O? (Use molar masses with at least 2 decimal places; report to two decimal places.)

steps.html: Molar masses (periodic table): C = 12.01, H = 1.01, O = 16.00.
Bottom (whole molar mass): 2(12.01) + 8(1.01) + 16.00 = 48.10 g/mol.

problems.q: What is the mass percent of phosphorus in sodium phosphite, Na₃PO₃?

steps.html: Molar masses (periodic table): Na = 22.99, P = 30.97, O = 16.00.
Top: one P = 30.97.

problems.q: What is the percent composition of Rh in Rh₂Cl₂H₄? (Rh = 102.91, Cl = 35.45, H = 1.01 g/mol; round to the ones place.)

steps.html: Molar masses are given in the problem.

problems.q: What is the percent composition of Cl in Rh₄Cl₃H₃? (Rh = 102.91, Cl = 35.45, H = 1.01 g/mol; round to the ones place.)

steps.html: Molar masses are given in the problem.

problems.q: What is the empirical formula of a compound that contains only cobalt and oxygen if an 8.29 gram sample contains 5.89 grams of cobalt?

steps.html: Oxygen by subtraction: 8.29 − 5.89 = 2.40 g O.
Molar masses (periodic table): Co = 58.93, O = 16.00.
Divide by the smallest (0.100): Co = 1, O = 1.5.
1.5 ends in .5 → × 2: Co = 2, O = 3 → Co₂O₃.

problems.q: A 6.341 g sample of a compound is found to have 1.433 grams of nitrogen and no other element except oxygen. What is the empirical formula of the compound?

steps.html: Oxygen by subtraction: 6.341 − 1.433 = 4.908 g O.
Molar masses (periodic table): N = 14.01, O = 16.00.
Divide by the smallest (0.1023): N = 1, O = 3.00.
Already whole numbers → NO₃.

problems.q: A hydrocarbon is found to contain 82.66% carbon and no other element except hydrogen. What is the empirical formula?

steps.html: Assume 100 g: 82.66 g C. Hydrogen by subtraction: 100 − 82.66 = 17.34 g H.
Molar masses (periodic table): C = 12.01, H = 1.01.
Divide by the smallest (6.883): C = 1, H = 2.49.

problems.q: A hydrocarbon is found to contain 53.3% carbon, 11.2% hydrogen, and no other element except oxygen. What is the empirical formula?

steps.html: Assume 100 g: 53.3 g C, 11.2 g H. Oxygen by subtraction: 100 − 53.3 − 11.2 = 35.5 g O.
Molar masses (periodic table): C = 12.01, H = 1.01, O = 16.00.
Divide by the smallest (2.219): C = 2.00, H = 5.00, O = 1.
Whole numbers; write C, H, then O → C₂H₅O.

problems.q: A hydrocarbon is found to contain 67.6% carbon, 9.94% hydrogen, and no other element except oxygen. What is the empirical formula?

steps.html: Assume 100 g: 67.6 g C, 9.94 g H. Oxygen by subtraction: 100 − 67.6 − 9.94 = 22.46 g O.
Molar masses (periodic table): C = 12.01, H = 1.01, O = 16.00.
Divide by the smallest (1.404): C = 4.01, H = 7.01, O = 1.
All within 0.1 → round → C₄H₇O.

problems.q: A hydrocarbon is found to contain 82.66% carbon and no other element except hydrogen. What is the empirical formula?

steps.html: Assume 100 g: 82.66 g C. Hydrogen by subtraction: 100 − 82.66 = 17.34 g H.
Molar masses (periodic table): C = 12.01, H = 1.01.
Divide by the smallest (6.883): C = 1, H = 2.49.
Same numbers as Q15, choices in a different order.

problems.q: A compound was discovered whose composition by mass is 85.6% C and 14.4% H. What is the empirical formula for this compound?

steps.html: Assume 100 g, so the percents become grams: 85.6 g C and 14.4 g H.
Molar masses (periodic table): C = 12.01, H = 1.01.
Divide by the smallest (7.13): C = 1, H = 2.00 → CH₂ (typed CH2).

problems.q: What is the total mass of the solution when 1 gram of salt is dissolved in 20 grams of water?

steps.html: Mass is conserved: solution = solute + solvent.
1 g + 20 g = 21 grams.

problems.q: A salt solution can be made more concentrated by boiling off some of the water. Which statement is true about the solution after this process?
choices: The amount of solute remains the same but the amount of solvent decreases.
The amount of solute and the amount of solvent increase.
The amount of solute and the amount of solvent decrease.
The amount of solute remains the same but the amount of solvent increases.
The amount of solvent remains the same but the amount of solute decreases.
problems.answer: The amount of solute remains the same but the amount of solvent decreases.

steps.html: Boiling removes the solvent (water). The salt (solute) doesn't boil off.
So the solute stays the same and the solvent decreases.

problems.q: The amount of solute in each beaker is represented by the number of black dots; the volume is shown on the side. In which beaker does the solute have the smallest concentration? (Count each dot as 1 mol.)
choices: More than one has the same smallest concentration

steps.html: Concentration = amount ÷ volume, so compute dots ÷ mL for each.
Smallest: Beaker 3 (the 15 mL beaker with 6 dots).

problems.q: There are different ways of representing molarity. Select all the answers that represent a 1.0 molarity solution.
choices: 1.0 moles popping out of a tunnel
problems.answer: 1.0 mol solute / 1 L solution, 1.0 molar, [1.0], 1.0 M

steps.html: Molarity = mol solute ÷ L solution, so "1.0 mol solute / 1 L solution" ✓.
Also written 1.0 molar, [1.0] (square brackets) and 1.0 M ✓.
Molality is a different unit; "1.0 L in a mol" is upside down; the others are made up ✗.

problems.q: What is the molarity of a solution of potassium bromide if 4.50 moles is dissolved in enough water to make 0.750 L of solution?

steps.html: Molarity formula: M = mol ÷ L.
Volume in liters: 0.750 L (already liters).
Sig figs: both have 3, so 6.00 M.

problems.q: What is the molarity of a solution if 42.7 moles is dissolved in enough water to make 7.7 L of solution? (Correct sig figs.)

steps.html: Molarity formula: M = mol ÷ L.
Volume in liters: 7.7 L (already liters).
Sig figs: 7.7 has 2, so 5.5 M.

problems.q: What is the molarity of a solution if 0.403 moles is dissolved in enough water to make 997.7 mL of solution? (Watch the volume unit; correct sig figs.)

steps.html: Molarity formula: M = mol ÷ L.
Volume in liters: 0.9977 L (997.7 mL ÷ 1000).
Sig figs: 0.403 has 3, so 0.404 M.

problems.q: Calculate the molarity (M) of a solution if 0.395 moles is dissolved in enough water to make 702.0 mL of solution. (Watch the volume unit; correct sig figs.)

steps.html: Molarity formula: M = mol ÷ L.
Volume in liters: 0.7020 L (702.0 mL ÷ 1000).
Sig figs: 0.395 has 3, so 0.563 M.

problems.q: What is the molarity of a solution prepared by dissolving 1.92 grams of sodium perchlorate (NaClO₄, molar mass = 122.44 g/mol) in enough water to make 125 mL of soln?

steps.html: Molar mass is given: NaClO₄ = 122.44 g/mol.
Volume in liters: 125 mL ÷ 1000 = 0.125 L.

problems.q: A solution is prepared by dissolving 17.0 g of potassium hydroxide (KOH, molar mass = 56.11 g/mol) in enough water to make 80.0 mL of solution. What is the molarity of this solution?

steps.html: Molar mass is given: KOH = 56.11 g/mol.
Volume in liters: 80.0 mL ÷ 1000 = 0.0800 L.
M = mol ÷ L = 3.79 M (3 sig figs).

problems.q: What is the molarity of a solution prepared by dissolving 4.90 grams of calcium nitrite [Ca(NO₂)₂, molar mass = 132.10 g/mol] in enough water to make a 123.0 mL soln? (Decimal form, correct sig figs, proper unit.)

steps.html: Molar mass is given: Ca(NO₂)₂ = 132.10 g/mol.
Volume in liters: 123.0 mL ÷ 1000 = 0.1230 L.

problems.q: A student removed 115.0 mL of a 0.139 M KCl solution. How many moles of KCl are in this sample?

steps.html: Rewrite molarity as 0.139 mol/L.
Start with the one-unit number, the volume in liters: 115.0 mL = 0.1150 L.
0.1150 L × 0.139 mol/L = 0.0160 mol (liters cancel).

problems.q: A student removed 140.0 mL of a 0.127 M KCl solution. How many moles of NaI are in this sample?

steps.html: Rewrite molarity as 0.127 mol/L.
Start with the one-unit number, the volume in liters: 140.0 mL = 0.1400 L.
0.1400 L × 0.127 mol/L = 0.0178 mol (liters cancel).
The KCl/NaI mix-up is a typo in the homework; the math is the same.

problems.q: How many grams of iron(III) nitrate (241.86 g/mol) are needed to prepare 150.0 mL of 0.132 M solution?

steps.html: Rewrite molarity as 0.132 mol/L; volume in liters: 150.0 mL = 0.1500 L.
Molar mass is given: 241.86 g/mol.

problems.q: How many grams of benzoic acid (C₇H₆O₂, molar mass = 122.13 g/mol) are required to make 597.0 mL of a 0.41 M solution? (Decimal form, correct sig figs, proper unit.)

steps.html: Rewrite molarity as 0.41 mol/L; volume in liters: 597.0 mL = 0.5970 L.
Molar mass is given: 122.13 g/mol.
Sig figs: 0.41 has 2 → 30 g.

problems.q: How many grams are needed to make 80.0 mL solution of 0.110 M aluminum nitrate [Al(NO₃)₃, molar mass = 213.01 g/mol]?

steps.html: Rewrite molarity as 0.110 mol/L; volume in liters: 80.0 mL = 0.0800 L.
Molar mass is given: 213.01 g/mol.

problems.q: A student needed 0.733 mol of HCl. What volume (in L) of 0.143 M HCl solution would she take in order to get this sample?

steps.html: Rewrite molarity as 0.143 mol/L.
Start with the one-unit number: 0.733 mol. Divide by molarity so mol cancels.

problems.q: A student needed 0.919 mol of KBr. What volume (in L) of 0.187 M KBr solution needs to be added to the graduated cylinder?

steps.html: Rewrite molarity as 0.187 mol/L.
Start with the one-unit number: 0.919 mol. Divide by molarity so mol cancels.

problems.q: A student planned to evaporate a solution so that only solid was left. They wanted to collect 3.41 g of lithium nitrate (LiNO₃, molar mass = 68.95 g/mol). What volume (in mL) of 0.911 M LiNO₃ solution needs to be in the flask?

steps.html: Molar mass is given: 68.95 g/mol.
Question wants mL: × 1000 = 54.3 mL.

problems.q: A student planned to evaporate a solution so that only solid was left. They wanted to collect 1.19 g of sodium fluoride (NaF, molar mass = 41.99 g/mol). What volume (in mL) of 0.945 M NaF solution needs to be in the flask? (Correct sig figs.)

steps.html: Molar mass is given: 41.99 g/mol.
Question wants mL: × 1000 = 29.99 mL.
3 sig figs → strictly 30.0 mL; eLearn accepted 29.9 mL.

problems.q: If a substance is diluted, what characteristics would you expect? (Select all that apply.)
choices: The solution will either have more volume or less solute.
The solution will have a darker vibrant color.
The numerical value of the molarity will go down.
If it is being created from a concentrated solution, the concentrated solution is put in a volumetric flask and then water is added so that it fills the entire flask to the very top.
problems.answer: More volume or less solute; molarity goes down

steps.html: Diluting means more volume or less solute ✓.
Molarity = mol ÷ L; bigger L → the molarity goes down ✓.
Color gets lighter, not darker ✗. You fill a volumetric flask to the graduation line, not the very top ✗.

problems.q: When doing dilution calculations, why should the volume units be the same?
choices: So that the unit will cancel.
So that you know everything will fit in any flask.
So that the dilution is faster in the lab.
problems.answer: So that the unit will cancel.

steps.html: Volumes sit on both sides of M₁V₁ = M₂V₂; matching units let them cancel.

problems.q: What is the molarity of a solution prepared by diluting 153 mL of 2.6 M acetic acid to 750.0 mL?

steps.html: Dilution equation: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.
M₁ = 2.6 M, V₁ = 153 mL, V₂ = 750.0 mL (same units ✓).
Sig figs: 2.6 has 2 → 0.53 M.

problems.q: A student prepared a solution by removing 20.0 mL of a 1.69 M HCl solution and transferring it to a 175.0 mL volumetric flask, then filled to the line with deionized water. What is the concentration of the new solution?

steps.html: Dilution equation: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.
Sig figs: 3 → 0.193 M.

problems.q: 50.0 mL of a 1.63 M solution was transferred to a 250.0 mL volumetric flask and diluted to the line with deionized water. What is the concentration of the new solution?

steps.html: Dilution equation: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.

problems.q: How many milliliters (mL) of 10.0 M nitric acid (HNO₃) would be required to prepare 127.0 mL of 0.31 M nitric acid solution? (Decimal form, correct sig figs, proper unit.)

steps.html: Dilution equation: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.
Sig figs: 0.31 has two → 3.9 mL.

problems.q: How many milliliters (mL) of a 10.0 M concentrated solution would be required to prepare 179.0 mL of a 0.31 M solution? (Decimal form, correct sig figs, proper unit.)

steps.html: Dilution equation: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.
Sig figs: two → 5.5 mL.

problems.q: A student wished to prepare 150.0 mL of a 0.650 M AgNO₃ solution. What volume (in mL) of 1.35 M AgNO₃ would she need to take?

steps.html: Dilution equation: M₁V₁ = M₂V₂.
Concentrated: M₁ = 1.35 M, V₁ = ?. Dilute: M₂ = 0.650 M, V₂ = 150.0 mL.

problems.q: Identify which elements should be diatomic and which should not. Mark the ones whose symbols are written correctly.
problems.answer: oxygen is O₂; potassium is K

steps.html: Diatomics: H₂, N₂, O₂, F₂, Cl₂, Br₂, I₂.
Nitrogen is diatomic, so "N" is wrong (should be N₂). Oxygen as O₂ is correct.
Boron isn't diatomic, so "B₂" is wrong. Potassium as K is correct.

problems.q: Select only the correctly written elements. There are seven correct answers.
problems.answer: Ba, Mg, I₂, Br₂, H₂, Na, Si

steps.html: Diatomics need the 2: I₂, Br₂, H₂ ✓; F, N, O are missing their 2 ✗.
Everything else is single: Ba, Mg, Na, Si ✓; Na₂, C₂, Li₂, Ne₂ are not diatomic ✗.

problems.q: Which correctly lists the precipitation reaction between aqueous copper(II) chlorite and aqueous lithium sulfide producing solid copper(II) sulfide and aqueous lithium chlorite? Make sure it's balanced.

steps.html: Chlorite from the polyatomic chart: ClO₂⁻. Copper(II) = Cu²⁺ → copper(II) chlorite = Cu(ClO₂)₂.
Sulfide ("-ide") = S²⁻; lithium = Li⁺ (column 1) → lithium sulfide = Li₂S (not Li₂SO₃, that's sulfite).
Products: Cu²⁺ + S²⁻ = CuS; Li⁺ + ClO₂⁻ = LiClO₂.
2 Li and 2 ClO₂ on the left → 2 LiClO₂. Equation: Cu(ClO₂)₂ + Li₂S → CuS + 2 LiClO₂.

problems.q: Classify the reaction (more than one may apply): 2 HgO (s) → 2 Hg (l) + O₂ (g)

steps.html: Only one reactant (no + on the left) → decomposition.
No fuel making CO₂/H₂O, no swap, no solid formed from solutions → nothing else applies.

problems.q: Classify the reaction (more than one may apply): KCl (aq) + AgNO₃ (aq) → AgCl (s) + KNO₃ (aq)

steps.html: Two compounds swap partners (K with NO₃, Ag with Cl) → double replacement.
A solid (s) forms from two solutions → also precipitation.

problems.q: Identify the type of reaction (no need to balance): S(s) + O₂(g) → SO₂(g)

steps.html: Two reactants make one product → synthesis.

problems.q: Identify the type of reaction (no need to balance): Pb(s) + AgNO₃(aq) → Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + Ag(s)

steps.html: An element is alone on each side (Pb in, Ag out) → single replacement.

problems.q: True or false: 1 mol of NaCl contains 6.022×10²³ NaCl units, and 1 mol of NaCl contains 1 mol of Na, so there are 6.022×10²³ Na atoms too.

steps.html: 1 mol = 6.022 × 10²³ of anything.
Each NaCl has one Na, so 1 mol NaCl → 1 mol Na → True.

problems.q: True or false: 1 mol of Cl₂ contains 6.022×10²³ Cl₂ molecules, and 1 mol of Cl₂ contains 1 mol of Cl, so there are 6.022×10²³ Cl atoms too.

steps.html: First part is right: 1 mol Cl₂ = 6.022 × 10²³ molecules.
But each Cl₂ has two Cl atoms: 1 mol Cl₂ → 2 mol Cl = 1.204 × 10²⁴ atoms → False.

problems.q: True or false: Mass is conserved in a chemical reaction because of the Law of Conservation of Mass, so the same number of each type of atom must show on each side of the reaction.

steps.html: Atoms aren't created or destroyed, so each atom count matches on both sides → True.

problems.q: True or false: Reactions must be balanced with coefficients because the Law of Conservation of Mass says total mass doesn't change; balancing puts the same number and types of atoms on both sides, so the mass on both sides is the same.

steps.html: Same atoms on both sides → same mass on both sides → True.

problems.q: Which of the following must be the same before and after a chemical reaction? (1) the sum of the masses, (2) the number of molecules, (3) the number of atoms of each type.
choices: 1) the sum of the masses of all substances involved
2) the number of molecules of all substances involved
3) the number of atoms of each type involved
4) both (1) and (3) must be the same
5) all of the answers (1), (2), and (3) must be the same
problems.answer: 4) both (1) and (3) must be the same

steps.html: Mass (1) and atoms of each type (3) are conserved.
Molecules (2) can change: 2 H₂ + O₂ → 2 H₂O goes from 3 molecules to 2. Answer: both (1) and (3).

problems.q: Why do we not change subscripts when balancing a chemical equation?
choices: We can change subscripts. We can't change coefficients.
Compounds composed of the same elements and having different subscripts are different substances.
It's fine to do it once in a while, but don't make a habit of it.
There's no real reason to, it's just something that is not done.
We never change subscripts because atoms are neither created nor destroyed. This is part of the law of conservation of matter.
problems.answer: Compounds composed of the same elements and having different subscripts are different substances.

steps.html: Subscripts are part of the identity of the substance.
Change them and you get a different substance: H₂O (water) → H₂O₂ (hydrogen peroxide).

problems.q: Lithium reacts vigorously with oxygen. Which set of coefficients balances the equation? Li + O₂ → Li₂O

steps.html: Count: left Li 1, O 2; right Li 2, O 1.
O first (no H here): 2 O on the left → 2 Li₂O. Now the right has 4 Li.
Fix Li: 4 Li. Final: 4 Li + O₂ → 2 Li₂O → 4, 1, 2.

problems.q: Solid aluminum reacts slowly with gaseous oxygen to produce solid aluminum oxide. Write and balance the equation. What are the whole-number coefficients on aluminum, oxygen, and aluminum oxide, in that order?

steps.html: Oxygen is diatomic: O₂.
Al³⁺ and O²⁻ criss-cross → Al₂O₃. Unbalanced: Al + O₂ → Al₂O₃.
O is 2 vs 3: swap them → 3 O₂ and 2 Al₂O₃ (6 O each).
2 Al₂O₃ has 4 Al → 4 Al. Final: 4 Al + 3 O₂ → 2 Al₂O₃.

problems.q: When Al₂O₃ (s) + H₂SO₄ (aq) → Al₂(SO₄)₃ (aq) + H₂O (l) is balanced with the smallest integers, what is the number in front of H₂O?

steps.html: Treat SO₄ as one group: right side has 3 SO₄ → 3 H₂SO₄.
That brings in 6 H → 3 H₂O.
Check O (outside SO₄): left 3 (in Al₂O₃), right 3 (in 3 H₂O) ✓. Answer: 3.

problems.q: When Br₂(l) + KI(aq) → I₂(aq) + KBr(aq) is balanced with the smallest integers, what is the number in front of KBr?

steps.html: Br₂ has 2 Br → 2 KBr.
That gives 2 K → 2 KI, which gives 2 I = I₂ ✓. Answer: 2.

problems.q: Balance: ___ H₃PO₄ + ___ NaOH → ___ Na₃PO₄ + ___ H₂O (enter four coefficients with no spaces or commas, like 1423).

steps.html: Keep PO₄ and OH as groups. PO₄: 1 and 1 ✓.
Na₃PO₄ has 3 Na → 3 NaOH.
Water: 3 H (from H₃PO₄) + 3 OH → 3 H₂O.
Coefficients 1, 3, 1, 3 → type 1313.

problems.q: Balance (type a 1 in any blank that needs it): Na + I₂ → NaI

steps.html: Iodine is diatomic: I₂ has 2 I → 2 NaI.
2 NaI has 2 Na → 2 Na. Blanks: 2, 1, 2.

problems.q: Balance (type a 1 in any blank that needs it): P₄ + O₂ → P₂O₃

steps.html: P: 4 on the left → 2 P₂O₃ (4 P).
2 P₂O₃ has 6 O → 3 O₂. Blanks: 1, 3, 2.

problems.q: Balance (type a 1 in any blank that needs it): N₄ + F₂ → NF₃

steps.html: N: 4 on the left → 4 NF₃.
4 NF₃ has 12 F → 6 F₂. Blanks: 1, 6, 4.

problems.q: Balance with whole numbers, keeping this product order (type a 1 if needed): C₂H₆ + O₂ → H₂O + CO₂

steps.html: C first: 2 C → 2 CO₂. H next: 6 H → 3 H₂O.
O last: 3 + 4 = 7 O needed, which is 3.5 O₂ (a fraction).
No fractions → double everything: 2 C₂H₆ + 7 O₂ → 6 H₂O + 4 CO₂.
Blanks in this order: 2, 7, 6, 4 (H₂O comes before CO₂ here).

problems.q: Balance (type a 1 in any blank that needs it): C + SO₂ → CS₂ + CO

steps.html: Start with S: CS₂ needs 2 S → 2 SO₂ (1 CS₂).
2 SO₂ has 4 O; O only goes to CO → 4 CO.
C last (lone element): 1 (in CS₂) + 4 (in CO) = 5 C. Blanks: 5, 2, 1, 4.

problems.q: Balance with whole numbers, keeping this product order (the fuel contains O; type a 1 if needed): C₃H₆O + O₂ → H₂O + CO₂

steps.html: O on the right: 3(2) + 3(1) = 9 O.
The fuel already brings 1 O, so O₂ supplies 8 → 4 O₂.

problems.q: Enter the formula, with state, of the missing substance Y (no coefficient; it is aq): Ba(NO₃)₂ + Li₂CO₃(aq) → Y + 2 LiNO₃(aq)

steps.html: Double replacement: Li ends up with NO₃, so Ba gets the CO₃.
Ba²⁺ (column 2) + CO₃²⁻ (chart) → charges cancel 1:1 → BaCO₃.
Atom check: Ba 1 = 1, NO₃ 2 = 2, Li 2 = 2, CO₃ 1 = 1 ✓. Type BaCO3 (aq) (really a solid, but the question says aq).

problems.q: When Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) + K₂CrO₄(aq) → PbCrO₄(s) + KNO₃(aq) is balanced with the smallest integers, what is the number in front of KNO₃?

steps.html: Keep NO₃ and CrO₄ as groups.
Left has 2 NO₃ → 2 KNO₃; that's 2 K, matching K₂CrO₄ ✓. Answer: 2.

problems.q: Predict the products (no need to balance): (NH₄)₂CO₃ + Al(NO₃)₃ →

steps.html: Ions from the chart: NH₄⁺, CO₃²⁻, NO₃⁻; Al is Al³⁺.
Double replacement: swap the negatives → NH₄ + NO₃, Al + CO₃.
NH₄⁺ + NO₃⁻ → NH₄NO₃. Al³⁺ + CO₃²⁻ criss-cross → Al₂(CO₃)₃.

problems.q: Predict the products (no need to balance): Ni(NO₃)₃(aq) + KBr(aq) →

steps.html: Ni holds three NO₃⁻, so here it is Ni³⁺. K is K⁺, Br is Br⁻.
Swap the negatives: K + NO₃, Ni + Br.
K⁺ + NO₃⁻ → KNO₃. Ni³⁺ + Br⁻ → NiBr₃.

problems.q: Predict the products (no need to balance): C₂H₆ + O₂ →

steps.html: Hydrocarbon + O₂ = combustion.
Combustion always makes CO₂ + H₂O.

problems.q: Predict the products (no need to balance): NaClO₃ + Mg →

steps.html: A lone metal + a compound → single replacement: Mg takes Na's place.
Mg is Mg²⁺ (column 2); chlorate is ClO₃⁻ (chart) → Mg(ClO₃)₂.
Na is left alone as Na. Products: Mg(ClO₃)₂ + Na.

problems.q: Match each reaction with its type (synthesis, decomposition, single replacement, double replacement, combustion): (a) 2 HgO → 2 Hg + O₂; (b) 4 C₂H₅ + 13 O₂ → 8 CO₂ + 10 H₂O; (c) HCl + AgNO₃ → AgCl + HNO₃; (d) 2 Na + H₂ → 2 NaH; (e) K₂O₃ + H₂SO₄ → K₂(SO₄)₃ + H₂O; (f) Mg + 2 NaNO₃ → Mg(NO₃)₂ + Na; (g) Mg(OH)₂ + 2 HNO₂ → Mg(NO₂)₂ + 2 H₂O

steps.html: Find combustion first (fuel + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O): (b) combustion.
One reactant: (a) decomposition. One product: (d) synthesis.
Lone element swaps in: (f) single replacement.
Two compounds swap partners: (c), (e), (g) double replacement.
